6.22.0.en: Ambrosiaster: And I will not go with one who wastes away with envy, for he has no fellowship in wisdom. [23]

6.22.1.en: The wise man urges us to love the light of wisdom, for the world’s light depends on the sun, which illumines outward things, but the light of wisdom gives the soul illumination to see hidden things and to recognize the mysteries of heaven, and to have sound judgment.

6.22.2.en: The wise man warns us against envy, which corrupts our eyes from seeing the true light. There is no fellowship between wisdom, which is in itself love for God and people, and envy, which bears no love for God or people. There is no enemy that corrupts wisdom in man’s life like envy, which has no portion in wisdom, or no fellowship with it.

6.22.3.en: St. Augustine spoke of the envy of beautiful Rachel, sharp of sight, toward Leah with the weak eyes, because the former was barren and the latter the Lord opened her womb to bear fruit and so become beloved by her husband. If we borrow, with some freedom, what St. Augustine wrote on this matter, we say that Rachel represents the man who devotes all his energies to the contemplative life alone, who has the sharp insight to enjoy the vision of divine mysteries, but does not serve. And Leah represents the earnest spiritual man who works in the Lord’s vineyard and so brings many sons to the Kingdom. For man cannot do without both lives together, that he may enjoy seeing the mysteries of God and work in His vineyard. Moreover, it does not befit one who devotes the greater part of his life to contemplation or to service to envy the other, but each completes the other, and each seeks what belongs to the other in a spirit of love.

6.23.0.en: The multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and the wise king the stability of the people. [24]

6.23.1.en: There is no salvation for the world without the true believers who enjoy wisdom. It is stated in the Epistle to Diognetus:

6.23.2.en: [Christians dwell in the world as the soul dwells in the body.

6.23.3.en: The soul is spread through the members of the body as Christians are spread through the cities of the world.

6.23.4.en: The soul dwells in the body, yet it is not of the visible body...

6.23.5.en: The flesh hates the soul and opposes it, though it receives no harm from it, except that it prevents it from plunging into the mire of pleasures. And the world hates Christians, not because they have wronged it, but because they stand against its perverse and corrupt desires. The soul loves the flesh that hates it, as Christians love those who hate them.

6.23.6.en: The soul is imprisoned in the body, yet without it the body would have no life, and Christians are bound in the prison of the world, yet without them the world has no existence and no life.]

6.23.7.en: Thus the true wise man, as he bears the Lord Christ in his heart, becomes a lover of mankind (of the world), longing for the salvation of all.

6.23.8.en: For wisdom is not theoretical knowledge but practical love for the whole world, and a longing for the edification of every soul and its enjoyment of eternal glory. So by saying “Be instructed by my words” he asks us that this discourse not turn into abstract philosophical thought, but into practical life and real benefit.

6.23.9.en: * “The multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world” (Wis 6:24). Thus the Apostle desires those to whom he speaks to be so: “I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil” (Rom 16:19). Now, since no one can be found so by himself, he cannot be wise by himself, but by being enlightened by the fullness of Him of whom it is written: “All wisdom cometh from the Lord” (Sir 1:1).

6.24.0.en: St. Augustine: Therefore receive instruction through my words, that you may profit by them. [25]

6.24.1.en: The wise man concludes his discourse here by revealing his purpose: he asks nothing for himself, but what is for their benefit and edification.

6.24.2.en: Grant me the spirit of wise fatherhood

6.24.3.en: * You bowed the heavens and came down to us, O King of kings and Lord of lords.

6.24.4.en: You came down to serve us, Your sinful servants, and did not seek service for Yourself.

6.24.5.en: You loved us, and humbled Yourself that You might raise us up.

6.24.6.en: How great is Your humility and Your love!

6.24.7.en: * Take from me the spirit of domination and the love of vainglory.

6.24.8.en: Grant me to possess You, that I may possess the spirit of humility and meekness and true love.

6.24.9.en: I love every person, and respect every person, whatever his age, even if he is one day old, and whatever his abilities and possibilities and position, even if he is destitute in everything.

6.24.10.en: Let Your Law be the law of my life, and Your wisdom the leader and guide of my depths, as of my conduct and my words.

6.24.11.en: * You have given me much, so much will be required of me.

6.24.12.en: I confess to You my laziness, my negligence and my unfaithfulness.

6.24.13.en: Who sets right my affair but You?

6.24.14.en: Who renews me but Your Holy Spirit?

6.24.15.en: Who helps me except Your surpassing grace?

6.24.16.en: * I long for the swiftness of Your coming, for I know that You are a compassionate Father, offering us fellowship in Your heavenly glories.

6.24.17.en: If You judge me, how shall I be justified before You?

6.24.18.en: There is nothing good in my flesh.

6.24.19.en: But I have full confidence in the riches of Your grace, and the power of Your Cross!

6.24.20.en: Come, and let Your fiery Spirit restore me with sanctification, that I may meet You, O Holy One.

6.24.21.en: * My God, I stand in amazement before Your initiative of love and Your condescension!

6.24.22.en: I see You ever present, wishing to be revealed before every soul, and seeking every person to give him Yourself, O divine Wisdom!

6.24.23.en: Yes, You are not far from anyone, but near to him, nearer than his parents or his children.

6.24.24.en: You rise early to us; grant us to rise early to You.

6.24.25.en: You sit at our doors; be pleased to rest in our depths.

6.24.26.en: * You watch over our salvation; nothing occupies You in heaven but our eternity.

6.24.27.en: Grant us to watch for the sake of our own souls.

6.24.28.en: You go about the roads like one who seeks us.

6.24.29.en: Grant us to long for You and enjoy meeting with You.

6.24.30.en: Grant me to know Your love and so love You.

6.24.31.en: Grant me by love to keep Your commandments, that I may draw near to You, and You dwell in me.

6.24.32.en: Grant me that You carry me in You, that I may enjoy Your Kingdom.

6.24.33.en: * I possess You, O King of kings, and so I count all that is in the world refuse.

6.24.34.en: I love You, and reign with You forever.

6.24.35.en: I possess You, O Wisdom of God, and so I know You and grasp Your mysteries.

6.24.36.en: I bear Your Spirit, and You make me wise, and by the wise You leaven the dough of this whole world.

7.0.0.en: 1 I am but a man who dies, like all other people, of the kind of the first who was formed of the earth, and I was fashioned as flesh in my mother’s womb, 2 and in the time of ten months I was made of blood by the seed of man, and the pleasure that accompanies sleep. 3 And when I was born I breathed this common air, and fell upon this common earth, and the first thing I uttered was weeping, as all do, 4 and I was brought up in swaddling clothes and with much care. 5 For there is no king that had any other beginning of birth than this; 6 but the entrance of all into life is one, and their departure is alike.

7.0.1.en: I too am a man liable to death, equal to all people, descended from the first who was formed of the earth, [1]

7.0.2.en: Concerning his temporal life the wise man confesses that he belongs to Adam, the first man, like all human beings, and is not of another origin that God should show him partiality. In this he opens the door of hope for all.

7.0.3.en: Perhaps some will ask: Does God have partiality, so that He gave Solomon wisdom in such a surpassing manner? Or did Solomon have a human nature different from ours, so that he enjoyed this wisdom?

7.0.4.en: The wise Solomon declares that the exalted wisdom he enjoyed is not due to any privilege in his nature, for all human beings, whatever their possibilities, abilities, position, culture, age or nationality, are equal, bearing the same human nature.

7.0.5.en: In the same spirit some have asked: Did the Apostle Paul have a nature different from the rest of mankind, that he attained this high spiritual stature, and occupied the first place in the service of the Gentiles, and the Holy Spirit worked in him as in a unique way?

7.0.6.en: And what we ask concerning the wise Solomon and the Apostle Paul we ask concerning many, such as the choice of Abraham as father of all nations, and David the king, that from his seed the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world, should come, and others.

7.0.7.en: St. John Chrysostom often answered such questions.

7.0.8.en: * When we are urged to practice some virtue, we must not say that these were partakers of a nature other than ours, or that they were not human. For this reason it is said of the great Elijah: “Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are” (Jas 5:17). Do you see that Elijah showed by his very sharing in sufferings that he was a man like us? Again it is said: “I myself also am a man of like passions with you” (cf. Wis 7:1). This gives assurance concerning the sharing of nature.

7.0.9.en: * The nature of the Apostle Paul was not different from our nature; nor was his soul different from our souls, nor did he live in another world, but dwelt in the same world and was subject to the same laws and customs, yet he surpassed all men in virtue, past and present.

7.0.10.en: Now, where are those who object to the difficulty of virtue and the ease of sin?

7.0.11.en: This man condemns them by his words: “For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor 17:4).

7.0.12.en: If his afflictions were bearable and light, how much more our afflictions, which if compared with his become as nothing or mere pleasures?

7.0.13.en: St. John Chrysostom: The writer declares that wisdom is for all, and that the true wise man desires all humanity to enjoy wisdom with him. This is contrary to what many of the pagans and philosophers held, who counted philosophy or the love of wisdom as limited to a chosen class. And many of them are careful to hide what they think is wisdom, as though it were their private property not to be approached.

7.0.14.en: * Let us despise all this and receive the spirit of wisdom in which there is no care, and hasten to obtain the wealth in which there is no deceit, and go to the pleasures of which it is said “the paradise of bliss.”

7.0.15.en: Origen: And I was fashioned as flesh in a mother’s womb, and in the time of ten months I was formed in blood, of the seed of a man.

7.1.0.en: And from the pleasure that accompanies sleep. [2]

7.1.1.en: By saying “fashioned as flesh in a mother’s womb,” the wise man highlights the hidden hand of the Creator working in the womb of every mother, for although the embryo is the fruit of a bodily relationship carrying pleasure between the spouses, it is not a sinful relationship, but God Himself who instituted marriage blesses it. So the embryo is of the creation of God, who cares for it, though it comes about by the natural law of marriage. It is said in the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations” (Jer 1:5).

7.1.2.en: He considered the period of pregnancy to be ten months, using in his calculations the lunar calendar (the lunar month equals 28 days) and not the solar.

7.2.0.en: And when I was born I too breathed the common air, and fell to the earth, as is the nature of man, and weeping was my first cry, as it is for all others. [3]

7.2.1.en: The wise Solomon does not forget the general gifts of God, which are priceless, in which rich and poor share, and which the child enjoys from his birth, such as the air he breathes, and the earth on which he lives, and even the first cry immediately after his birth, without which the lungs do not open to work.

7.2.2.en: How beautiful to remember the free divine gifts shared among all human beings.

7.2.3.en: Many of the Fathers of the Church lift up their hearts in thanksgiving to God who did not entrust any man with the precious gifts but offered them general and common to all, such as water, air, the sun, etc., while He left the luxuries such as gold, silver, precious stones and costly garments to private ownership, that the rich might practice the virtue of giving, and the poor the virtue of thanks to those who give them these things.

7.2.4.en: * You set up the heaven for me as a roof, and fixed the earth for me to walk upon...

7.2.5.en: The Liturgy: St. Gregory the Theologian: * What does the Apostle mean when he says: “But in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy” (1 Tim 6:17)? God gives us abundantly all the necessary things more than money, such as air and water and fire and the rays of the sun and things of this kind. Yet it cannot be said that the rich man has more rays of sun than the poor, nor can it be said that the rich man breathes more air than the poor. All these things are available to all in a common way and equally. Why did God make the greater and more important things, those that supply us with life, common to all, while the lesser and very base things, that is money, are not common to people? This is what I would like to ask. That He might preserve our life and open before us the way of virtue; and on the other hand, if the necessities of life were not common, the rich would have seized them in their usual greed, and deprived the poor of them. For if they had done this with money, how much more would they have done the same with these things. And on the other hand if money were common and available to all, there would have been no opportunity for giving alms, and no incentive for doing good.

7.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom: And I was brought up in swaddling clothes and cares. [4]

7.3.1.en: It is wonderful that Solomon, the greatest king of his time, never let go of the picture of himself as an infant in swaddling clothes, whom people carry as they wish. This sight establishes in him the spirit of humility, and removes from him any arrogance.

7.4.0.en: For no king has any other beginning of existence than this. [5]

7.4.1.en: The wise man calls all kings to review themselves, how they began life, that they may behave toward the people in a spirit of brotherhood or tender fatherhood, because all have the same beginning, without distinction between this one and that.

7.5.0.en: But there is one entrance for all into life, and one for their departure. [6]

7.5.1.en: What is the entrance into life but that we were born naked, and what is our exit but the door of death, where we go out of the world naked as we entered. As Job said: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21).

7.5.2.en: * [In a letter of consolation to Alexandra, when she lost her son, he wrote:]

7.5.3.en: The divine decree removed him from us, and transferred him to the better life; therefore I remove the cloud of grief from myself, and I urge you, dear friend, to scatter the pain of your sorrows by the power of reason, and to bring yourself in this hour of need to the enchantment of the word of God...

7.5.4.en: I know how very sad and painful this matter is. When a man has experienced the value of the thing he loves and is suddenly deprived of it, and falls in a moment from a state of happiness to misery.

7.5.5.en: But as for those who have been given sound feeling and use their energies with sound reasoning, they do not expect the coming of any unseen human event. For nothing human is stable, nothing is lasting, neither beauty nor wealth nor health and honor. None of all these things, even for those of very high classes... I know, dear friend, that you know all this. And I beg you to contemplate human nature, and you will find it mortal, and it received the destiny of death from the beginning.

7.5.6.en: God said to Adam: “Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 19:3)...

7.5.7.en: The Holy Bible tells us: “One entrance for all into life, and one for their departure” (Gen 6:7)

7.5.8.en: And everyone who is born looks forward to the grave. Not all live the same length of time. Some reach the end very quickly, others during the vigor of manhood, and some after they have experienced old age.

7.6.0.en: 7 Then I wished, and prudence was given me; and I called, and the spirit of wisdom came upon me. 8 So I preferred her before scepters and thrones, and counted wealth as nothing in comparison with her, 9 neither compared I unto her any precious stone, for all gold in respect of her is a little sand, and silver shall be counted as clay before her. 10 And I loved her above health and beauty, and took her to me for a light, for her brightness never sets, 11 and all kinds of good came to me with her, and innumerable riches I received from her hands. 12 And I rejoiced in all these, because wisdom is their leader, and I knew not that she is the mother of them all. 13 I learned her without guile, and I share her without envy, and her riches I do not hide. 14 For she is a treasure unto men that never faileth, and those who have profited by it were made partakers in the love of God, for the gifts of discipline brought them near to Him.

7.7.s.en: a. Preferring her to the throne and wealth

7.7.0.en: For this cause I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called, and the spirit of wisdom came to me. [7]

7.7.1.en: What distinguishes the wise Solomon is that he is a man of prayer, who believes that nothing fills his being but God, and nothing satisfies even his mental needs but God, the giver of wisdom and understanding, so he never ceases to pray to the Father of lights.

7.7.2.en: St. James the Apostle says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17).

7.7.3.en: * James calls God “the Father of intellectual lights,” meaning that He is the Enlightener of rational beings, for He is the giver of these divine gifts, offering them to human beings, and as James says they are the best gifts, without blemish and perfect beyond doubt.

7.7.4.en: St. Didymus the Blind: * No man deserves to receive anything from the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift, except that he receives what he does not deserve.

7.7.5.en: * This is the wisdom that restrains the tongue, coming down from above, and not springing from a human heart. Does anyone dare to snatch it from the grace of God, without the swelling of pride, and put it in the authority of man?

7.7.6.en: St. Augustine: Origen sees that the life of the believer is a journey from this world to the heavenly things, where he needs the light of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, who shines upon him gradually in this world, so he enters from glory to glory, and experiences the heavenly life until he reaches the Heavenly One Himself, the Creator of all and the giver of every good gift.

7.7.7.en: * The soul ascends gradually to the heavens after the resurrection. It does not reach the highest point at once, but through many stages, where it is illumined progressively by the light of wisdom until it reaches the Father of lights Himself.

7.7.8.en: Origen: Prayer is the way to enjoy wisdom, for it is fellowship with the wisdom of God, our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. No one can reach Him and know Him and be united with Him except by the Holy Spirit of God.

7.8.0.en: So I preferred her before scepters and thrones, and counted wealth as nothing in comparison with her. [8]

7.8.1.en: When man possesses divine Wisdom, he becomes truly a spiritual king united with the King of kings. So he despises every temporal honor offered him, or authority or wealth. He finds in his Christ every inward honor and glory and wealth, therefore the Psalmist sings, saying: “The glory of the king’s daughter is in her chamber, her clothing is woven with gold” (Ps 13:45).

7.8.2.en: Since we have received the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, as His body, and He has become our Head, therefore we enjoy great honor, for our Head is the King of kings and Lord of lords. By this we receive an honor that surpasses even many of the heavenly ones, as St. John Chrysostom says:

7.8.3.en: * Do you know “the riches of the glory of his inheritance”? Do you know the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe (Eph 19:1)? Do you know the hope of your calling?

7.8.4.en: Let us honor our Head, so that what belongs to the Head is reflected upon the body, the Head to whom all things are subject. By this picture we ought to be better than the angels, and by this we are honored more than all of them...

7.8.5.en: For it is not a crown that is placed upon our heads, but something greater, Christ Himself has become our Head, and yet we do not care about this.

7.8.6.en: The angels honor this Head, and also the archangels and all those heavenly powers. Are we, who are His body, not in awe of Him for some reason or another?

7.8.7.en: St. John Chrysostom: * God does not want to give riches to the outward man and leave the inner man in want; He offers invisible riches in an invisible way.

7.9.0.en: St. Augustine: Neither compared I unto her any precious stone, for all gold in respect of her is a little sand, and silver shall be counted as clay before her. [9]

7.9.2.en: For wisdom is better than pearls, and all the jewels are not equal to it” (Prov 8:11).

7.9.3.en: “How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!” (Prov 16:16).

7.9.4.en: The true believer enjoys fellowship with the wisdom of God, so he sees the invisible heavenly things and despises the temporal things.

7.9.5.en: As the wisdom of God shines with its light upon the human soul, it is illumined, and perceives the reality of things, that there is no ground of comparison between divine Wisdom and temporal things, so man sees himself very rich, not in need to gather anything, and even counts precious stones as nothing, and gold as sand, and silver as clay.

7.9.6.en: * Faith sees beyond the sight of the bodily eye. Bodily eyes are not in the heads of the wise alone, but even of the unwise.

7.10.s.en: b. Preferring her to health and beauty

7.10.0.en: And I loved her above health and beauty, and chose to take her before the light, for the light that comes from her does not grow dim. [10]

7.10.1.en: In a letter that St. John Chrysostom sent to his friend in the ascetic life Theodore, when the beauty of a young woman of fair form called Hermoine had seduced him, so that he fell in love with her and wished to marry her, he pointed to man’s concern for the beauty of the body, while God seeks the surpassing beauty of the soul, which is within the ability of the believer by divine grace.

7.10.2.en: * Truly God fixed bodily beauty within the limits of nature (that is, man cannot shape his body), but the grace of the soul is set free from confinement and slavery, ascending from this state, as it rises far above any bodily harmony, and it depends in this on us (that is, our will) and on the grace of God.

7.10.3.en: So our Lord, being merciful, honored our race in this special way, leaving it to nature to deal with the shaping of small matters (the body) which do not contribute much to our benefit. Under its authority are unimportant things, but as for us, He made us artists in what concerns the things that are truly important (that is, by our will we surrender to the grace of God to form the soul and beautify it).

7.10.4.en: For if God had left it to us to shape our bodies, we would have become increasingly anxious, and wasted all our time on things that do not profit, and consequently we would have neglected the soul exceedingly.

7.10.5.en: And despite what we are, in not being given this authority (in choosing and shaping our bodies), we make tremendous efforts, and since we cannot obtain true bodily beauty, we contrive cleverly many imitations, using powders and dyes, and adorning ourselves with wigs, and jewelry, and the use of pencils for the eyebrows... and many tricks. If we had been given the ability to shape the body truly, would we have the time to devote to the soul and to the weighty matters?!

7.10.6.en: If we suppose that this was our work, we would have no other work, but would spend all our time in it, adorning the maidservant (the body) with countless ornaments, leaving her mistress (the soul) in a deformed and neglected state. For this reason God relieved us of the useless work, placing in us the power to work in the noble element (the soul).

7.10.7.en: So he who cannot change his ugly body into a beautiful form can raise the soul, even if it had descended to the utmost limits of ugliness, to bring it to the summit of beauty. And he not only makes it loved and desired by the righteous but makes it so by God Himself, the Lord of all and their God; the Psalmist says when he spoke concerning this beauty: “So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty” (Ps 45:11).

7.10.8.en: St. John Chrysostom: We realize that divine Wisdom seeks the surpassing beauty of the soul which is of His work, so we are not occupied with our bodily beauty.

7.10.9.en: * The bride continues her discourse with her disciples, and speaks of an astonishing truth about herself so that we may know how great is the Bridegroom’s love for the sons of men, who bestowed beauty on the beloved bride through such love. She says: “Do not marvel that the Truth loved me.” Though I became black because of sin and dwelt in the shadows because of my works, the Bridegroom made me beautiful through his love, for he exchanged his beauty for my disgrace (Isa 2:53-3; Phil 7:2). After he bore the filth of my sin, he allowed me to share his purity and bestowed his beauty upon me. He turned my repulsive appearance into beauty, he showed me his love...

7.10.10.en: Though we became darkness because of sin, God has bestowed upon us beauty and radiance through His surpassing grace. When night reigns and darkness envelops everything, we find that although some things become bright by nature when day comes, comparing them with the darkness does not apply to the things that were formerly darkened with blackness. And so the soul passes from error to truth, and the form of its dark life is changed into surpassing grace. The Apostle Paul, the bride of Christ, passed from darkness to light, for he says to his disciple Timothy (1 Tim 13:1), as the bride to her maidservant, that he had become worthy to be beautiful, because he was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor and a slanderer and darkened. And the Apostle Paul also says that Christ came into the world to enlighten those in darkness. Christ did not call the righteous but sinners to repentance, who made them shine as lights in the world (Phil 15:2), by the bath of the second birth that washed them from their first black form...

7.10.11.en: The bride enthusiastically encourages the daughters of Jerusalem as she describes to them the goodness of the Bridegroom who receives the black soul and returns it to the image of the first beauty by fellowship with Him. So he who was “as the tents of Kedar” becomes a shining dwelling for the true Solomon, that is, the King of peace dwells in him. Therefore the text says: “I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem.”

7.10.12.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa: As we enjoy the eternal divine light, the wisdom of God, we count every light in the world as nothing.

7.10.13.en: * One lamp I look upon, and by its light I am illumined, and now I am in amazement, rejoicing spiritually, for within me is the spring of life, He who is the goal of the imperceptible world!

7.10.14.en: * Bear the yoke of your Lord in your heart, and the wonder of His majesty in your mind always, and the radiant light of your Lord who illumines your heart will pour into you!

7.10.15.en: The Spiritual Elder: * O invisible light!

7.10.16.en: O splendor that no other splendor beholds!

7.10.17.en: You are the light before which all created lights vanish!

7.10.18.en: You are the splendor before which all external splendor is extinguished!

7.10.19.en: You are the “Light,” the source of all lights, and the “Splendor,” the spring of all splendor!

7.10.20.en: You are the light and the splendor; before You all lights become darkness, and all brightness is to You nothing but darkness!

7.10.21.en: You are the splendor by whom darkness becomes light, and by You the darkness glitters with brightness!

7.10.22.en: You are the highest light, no cloud veils You, no vapor hinders You; night is unable to draw its darkness over You, no barrier hinders You and no shadows drown You!

7.10.23.en: Finally, You are the light that continually illumines the inner creation; swallow me up in the abyss of Your majesty, that I may behold all Your depths, by the power of the splendor of Your very divinity, and the work of the splendor reflected upon me from You!

7.10.24.en: Never leave me, lest my ignorance increase and my evils multiply, for without You I become empty and wretched!

7.10.25.en: Without You no one has any goodness, for You alone are the truth and the true goodness!

7.10.26.en: This I confess; and this is what I know, O God my God, that wherever I am found without You I have nothing but misery, within as without, for every wealth that is not divine is to me utter poverty!

7.11.0.en: And all good things came to me with her, and innumerable riches in her hands. [11]

7.11.1.en: Father Marius Victorinus comments on the Apostle’s saying “the manifold wisdom of God” (Eph 10:3), saying: The promises are so great: forgiveness of sins, the promise of heaven, eternal life and glorification, and our inheritance with Christ Himself in His resurrection from the dead, indeed in His very death (as a gift to us). All this makes the wisdom of God manifold.

7.11.2.en: * Without the Lord Jesus and the working of His divine power, no one can know the mysteries of God and His wisdom, or obtain true wealth, and become a Christian. For the wise brave warriors and philosophers of God are those who are led by the divine power and are nourished by it and are disciplined in the man who speaks by it.

7.12.0.en: St. Macarius the Great: And I rejoiced in all these good things, because wisdom goes before them, and I did not know that she is the mother of them. [12]

7.12.1.en: * Let me cleave to You, for You alone are good, and without You there is no existence for good! Be all my happiness, O All-good!

7.12.2.en: * Are You not the supreme Good, and every good is derived from You?!

7.12.3.en: * The heart that does not seek You, what does it seek?! Does it seek wealth that does not fill the world or does it seek created things... And what is this desire for created things but a continual hunger?! Whoever possesses them, his soul remains unsatisfied, for it cannot be satisfied except by You, O my God, since You created it in Your image...

7.12.4.en: O Lord my God... O You who are supreme in power... I have now known the place of Your delight. It is the soul created in Your image, in Your likeness, that which seeks none but You, and longs for none but You...!

7.13.0.en: St. Augustine: And what I learned with sincerity I share liberally, and I do not hide her wealth. [13]

7.13.1.en: * What do you seek, O my wretched soul?!

7.13.2.en: If you want wisdom, you find Jesus the source of wisdom and its spring, indeed He is Wisdom itself!

7.13.3.en: And if you seek strength and power, He is the Almighty!

7.13.4.en: If you search for pleasure and delight, He is the spring of true joy!

7.13.5.en: If you long for intoxication, His love intoxicates the soul!

7.13.6.en: If you hunger for bread, He is the bread of life!

7.13.7.en: And if you are passionate for wealth, He is the Creator of all!

7.13.8.en: And if you want rest, you find in Him alone your rest...! Receive Him, for you have no one else to satisfy you.

7.14.s.en: d. Realizing that she is the way of friendship with God

7.14.0.en: For she is a treasure unto men that never faileth, and those who have possessed it became friends of God, the gifts that come from learning commending them to Him. [14]

7.14.1.en: As Solomon justifies the greatness of wisdom, and his esteem of it above the throne on which he sits and wealth, he links wisdom with discipline. Man cannot enjoy wisdom unless he accepts the Lord’s disciplines for his edification.

7.14.2.en: * When we rejoice in prayer, our mind is quieted not by the possessions of the world but by the light of truth... Our souls rejoice in God, and are not far from Him, for as it is said: “In him we live, and move, and have our being” (Acts 17:28), but as a brother and as a neighbor, as a friend to me! (Ps 35:14).

7.14.3.en: St. Augustine: * There is no kinship or bond like the kinship of the soul to God, or the kinship of God to the soul.

7.15.s.en: 3. Asking for divine inspiration to speak of her

7.15.0.en: 15 And God has granted me to express what is in my mind, and to conceive in my thought what befits His gifts; for He is the guide to wisdom and the instructor of the wise. 16 And in His hand are we, and our words, and all prudence, and the knowledge of what is made.

7.15.1.en: May God grant me to speak as is fitting, and to conceive in my mind what befits what I have received of gifts, for He is the guide of wisdom and the director of the wise. [15]

7.15.2.en: As Solomon expressed his desire that people share with him in enjoying wisdom for their benefit, before describing wisdom to them he lifted his heart to God asking Him to give him a word that supports him to speak of wisdom.

7.15.3.en: * Perhaps an alert reader will object, saying: “If Paul knows in part and prophesies in part, and sees now as through a glass, darkly (1 Cor 12:13), how then was the mystery of God revealed to him as to the Ephesians in all wisdom and prudence (Eph 9:1)...? They did not learn this mystery by themselves in all wisdom and prudence, but God who is in all wisdom and prudence reveals the mystery to us as much as we are able to take in.”

7.16.0.en: St. Jerome: And in His hand are we and our words, and all wisdom and all knowledge of the sciences of craftsmanship. [16]

7.16.1.en: * Let our discourse be of help to you (O widows), and let everything be devoted to the grace of God, as it is written: “For in his hand are both we and our words” (Wis 7:16).

7.17.s.en: 4. Sciences and knowledge are gifts of divine wisdom

7.17.0.en: 17 And He gave me certain knowledge of the cosmos, that I might know the order of the world and the powers of the elements, 18 the beginning of times and their end and what is between them, the change of conditions and the alteration of seasons, 19 the cycles of the years and the positions of the stars, 20 the natures of animals and the dispositions of beasts and the blasts of the winds and the thoughts of men, the diversity of plants and the powers of drugs. 21 So I knew all things, both hidden and manifest, for He it is who gave me certain knowledge of the creatures, that I might know the order of the world and the working of the elements [17]

7.17.1.en: The beginning of times and their end and what is between them, and the succession of the equinoxes and the change of seasons. [18]

7.18.0.en: The cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, [19]

7.19.0.en: The natures of animals and the instincts of beasts, and the violence of winds and the thoughts of men, the kinds of plants and the properties of roots. [20]

7.19.1.en: Solomon owes to God his enjoyment of wisdom and the spirit of counsel, and also his acquaintance with many sciences such as astronomy, and the arts, and the crafts. It is stated in First Kings: “And his fame was in all nations round about. And he spake three thousand proverbs: and his songs were a thousand and five. And he spake of trees, from the cedar tree that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall: he spake also of beasts, and of fowl, and of creeping things, and of fishes. And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, which had heard of his wisdom” (1 Kgs 4:31-34). Solomon knew the natures of animals and their instincts, and it is stated in Jewish tradition and Jewish popular folklore that he understood the languages of animals and birds. He also understood their habits, and composed proverbs making use of their habits.

7.19.2.en: * Behold, you see that the heart of man, which is able to comprehend all this, is not small. Realize that his greatness is not measured by the size of the body but by the power of his comprehension. He is able to comprehend such great knowledge of the truth!

7.20.0.en: Origen: So I knew all that is secret and all that is manifest, [21]

7.20.1.en: The wise Solomon attributes his knowledge of the habits of animals and birds and what goes on in nature to God Himself, as the Great Architect and Creator who knows all the secrets of nature, and who gave him wisdom to become acquainted with these things.

7.20.2.en: But what is in the hearts and minds of people God did not reveal to Solomon; these God does not entrust to any being except within very narrow limits for the fulfillment of His plan. He covers humanity, and does not expose what is in man’s conscience and feelings and thoughts; but they will be exposed on the day of judgment when man refuses to cover himself with God’s mercies and grace through returning to God by repentance.

7.20.3.en: * [In speaking of the sons of Seth, who are the sons of God who saw the daughters who were of the offspring of Cain, and desire was kindled in them because of their beauty] These fell away from the true study of natural philosophy which they had received from their ancestors, where the first man (Adam) pursued the study of all nature and was able to obtain it clearly, and handed it on to his successor on sure foundations, as much as he saw of the world at its beginning, when man was still in his tenderness and simplicity, as one in whom was not only the perfection of this wisdom, but also the grace of prophecy which was given him by divine revelation, so that while he was dwelling in this world untaught he gave names to all living creatures, and knew not only the fury of all kinds of animals and serpents and their poisons, but also distinguished the kinds of plants and trees and the natures of stones and the changing of the seasons which he had not yet experienced.

7.20.4.en: He was able to say well: “The Lord gave me certain knowledge of the creatures, that I might know the order of the world, and the working of the elements, the beginning of times and their end and what is between them, the succession of the equinoxes and the change of seasons, the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of animals and the instincts of beasts, the melodies of the spirits and the thoughts of men, the kinds of plants and the properties of roots, so I knew all that is secret and all that is manifest” (Wis 17:7-21).

7.21.s.en: 5. Wisdom is a reflection of the divine light

7.21.0.en: 21 For wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me. 22 For in her is the understanding and holy Spirit, the only-begotten, of many qualities, gentle, swift of motion, eloquent, pure, luminous, sound, loving the good, keen, free, beneficent, 23 loving mankind, steadfast, firm, tranquil, mighty, all-watching, who penetrates all spirits that are understanding, pure, and gentle. 24 For wisdom is swifter in motion than every moving thing; for her purity she enters and penetrates all things. 25 For she is the vapor of the power of God, and the pure outflow of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled mingles with her, 26 for she is the radiance of the eternal light, and the pure mirror of the working of God, and the image of His goodness. 27 She can do all things, and she is one, and renews all things while she remains in herself. And in every generation she dwells in holy souls, and produces friends of God and prophets, 28 for God loves no one but him who dwells with wisdom. 29 She is more radiant than the sun, and higher than every position of the stars, and when compared with light she goes before it, 30 for light is followed by night, but evil does not overcome wisdom.

7.21.1.en: For the artificer of all things taught me, and she is wisdom.

7.21.2.en: For in her is an intelligent spirit, holy, only, manifold, subtle, mobile, piercing, pure, plain, undefiled, loving the good, keen. [22]

7.22.0.en: Free, beneficent, loving mankind, steadfast, secure, at ease, able to do all things, overseeing all things, penetrating all spirits, the intelligent, and the pure, and the most subtle. [23]

7.22.1.en: Some see that Solomon the wise presents in verses 22 and 23 twenty-one attributes of wisdom which reveal the perfections of God. For if the number 7 refers to perfection, and the number 3 to the divine hypostases, then the number 21 (7×3) refers to the perfection of God.

7.22.2.en: When the Holy Bible offers us attributes of a divine hypostasis such as the wisdom of God or the Son of God, it offers in our human language what cannot be expressed in any language. Because God cannot be spoken of in a human language, He offers us the attributes with which we come into contact and interact and live by.

7.22.4.en: * We do not believe that when He emptied Himself, He, being Spirit, became something else. Rather, He laid aside for a time the dignity of His majesty, clothing Himself in a human body. Only by becoming in human form could He become the Savior of mankind. Note that when the sun is covered by a cloud its brightness is hindered but it does not become dark. The light of the sun, which spreads over all the earth, penetrates everything with its brilliant shining, is hidden by a small cloud which hinders it but it is not removed. So also this man whom Jesus Christ became (put on) as being our Savior, meaning that God and the Son of God was not diminished but hid His divinity in him for a few moments.

7.22.5.en: Gregory, bishop of Elvira: 2. Intelligent or wise (v. 22).

7.22.6.en: He offers us the wisdom of God Himself, that we may possess Him, and by Him we become wise, by Him we know God and know His divine mysteries, and come to Him.

7.22.7.en: * The Apostle says that the power of God is eternal and His divinity (Rom 20:1). For it is written that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 24:1)... It is written: “No man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Jn 6:14). So what you understand concerning the Father... you could never have understood without the help of the Son, and no understanding can ascend to the knowledge of the Father except through the Son.

7.22.8.en: St. Ambrose: 3. Holy, with nothing defiled entering into it (vv. 22, 25).

7.22.9.en: * The words “Be perfect” were addressed to Abraham, to whom was given the spirit of wisdom, holy, wonderful in his gentleness, pure... Whoever receives wisdom cannot but be good and perfect, as he possesses every virtue and is an icon of goodness.

7.22.10.en: * If the Spirit has no sin, He is God. How could he sin who Himself forgives sins (Jn 20:22)? Therefore He does not commit sin, and if He is without sin He is not a creature, for every creature is subject to the possibility of sin, but the eternal divinity alone is without sin and holy.

7.22.11.en: St. Ambrose: * By means of prayer fellowship is generated in the holiness of God in those who are counted worthy of it... The man who forces himself every day to persevere in prayer is kindled with divine love, and burns with a fiery desire of spiritual love toward God, and receives the grace of the perfect sanctification of the spirit.
